Jokdeam
JOK-dee-am
proper noun
Hebrew Yoqdeam, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “burning of the people”; a town in the hill country of Judah, named once.

Biblical Definition

Jokdeam was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed once between Jezreel and Zanoah: “And Jezreel, and Jokdeam, and Zanoah” (Josh 15:56). It lay in the highland district of Judah, in the same country as Maon and Carmel and Ziph, the wilderness where David hid from Saul and where Nabal fed his flocks. Nothing of Jokdeam’s particular history is told; it is a name and no more. Yet these obscure hill-towns together make up the inheritance of Judah, the royal tribe from which the Lion of the tribe of Judah would come. The whole roll of them is sealed with the words, “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families” (Josh 15:20). Jokdeam preaches, with all its silent neighbours, that God keeps a record of what men forget. The town whose deeds are lost to history is not lost to God, who numbers the hairs of the head and writes the names of His people in the Lamb’s book of life. The obscurity of Jokdeam is a comfort to every hidden and forgotten saint: the LORD forgets nothing that is His.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the hill country of Judah, named once (Josh 15:56); a comfort that God keeps a record of what men forget, and forgets nothing that is His.

JOKDEAM, a town in the hill country of Judah.

Named once, with Jezreel and Zanoah (Josh 15:56).

The meaning of the name is uncertain.

It lay in the highland district of Maon, Carmel, and Ziph.

A comfort that God forgets nothing and no one that is His.

Modern Corruption

An obscure hill-country town of Judah; it recovers the comfort that God keeps a record of what men forget and forgets no hidden saint.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A town named once and never again draws no modern quarrel. Its very obscurity is its message: what history forgets, the God of the record does not.

The principle to recover is that God forgets nothing that is His. The hill-towns of Judah whose stories are lost are yet written in His word for ever. So the hidden believer, whose labours are unseen and whose name is unknown to the world, is known to God, whose book records every tear and every faithful deed. Not one good thing the LORD promised failed (Josh 21:45); nor shall the least of His saints be forgotten at the last.
